This points to the dynamic nature of the industry — as customers, competitors, and new entrants to the market, all want a seat at the table. 6 We’ve strived to be member-driven and member-focused from the start, which has contributed to our success. Our members, in turn, have invested considerable time in contributing to our technology roadmap, spreading the word about PowerAmerica, contributing to education efforts, and helping us address their challenges. Several new companies have asked to join because a current member told them about PowerAmerica and what we do. Our Member Advisory Committee (MAC) provides a voice for industry and a forum for important discussions about governance, financial planning, and technical direction; this is well-demonstrated by our portfolio of 26 Member Initiated Projects (MIP) completed over the past four years , which were funded solely with member dues — and focused on member’s specific technical challenges. From selecting the technical topics to reviewing proposals and reviewing the project’s results, the MIPs represent the voice of industry in guiding research that addresses crosscutting challenges to wider WBG adoption. MIPs typically team a university together with a company or national lab — helping to ensure that the task is appropriately focused and the results and know-how are shared appropriately. Members have also supported some of our undergraduate student scholarships and contributed their valuable time to our education efforts, such as the annual WBG Short Course, bi-annual tutorials, technical webinars, and special panels at large semiconductor industry conferences. Member dues have helped sustain PowerAmerica after DoE funding ended in April 2021. Membership has grown steadily and now stands at 90. Importantly, the growth has been mainly in companies in the core device fabrication and power electronic integration sectors of the market. Most new members are customers or suppliers of existing members. EDUCATION & WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT PowerAmerica’s Education and Workforce Development (EWD) program has perhaps had the broadest reach and most lasting impact of all our endeavors. As the table below indicates, hundreds of students — and thousands of working professionals — have benefited from our technical webinars, tutorials, WBG Short Courses, and other EWD programming. In the early budget periods, our EWD activities included STEM activities for K-12 and community college instructors. For example, we visited middle school campuses to hold competitions for student-built model EV cars and teach classroom lessons with tabletop science kits, and we gave community college instructors hands-on lab activities and guidance on electric energy principles. Since the third year of operation under DOE support, all activities have focused on university-level students and working professionals, as these two groups represent a more targeted use of resources 7 and better meet industry’s near-term needs.
